item.title: Sunday, July 5, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s digest highlights a community deeply invested in the “co-design” paradigm: the idea that our hardware (detectors, triggers) and our theory (SMEFT operators, GPD extraction) can no longer be optimized in isolation. We are seeing a concerted push to embed heavy computational machinery—like GPU-accelerated Hough transforms or neural-network-optimized trigger templates—directly into the infrastructure of proposed high-luminosity facilities like the STCF.

The theoretical mood is equally rigorous. The field is moving beyond broad-brush searches for new physics toward a granular, “precision-first” approach. Whether it’s the refined mapping of gluon GPDs for the EIC, or the emergence of “protected” composite Higgs states defined by lattice-verified collective kernels, the emphasis is on identifying observables that are resilient to the noise of standard model backgrounds. It is a day characterized by meticulous technical progress, where the tools of the trade—from lattice QCD to real-time pattern matching—are being sharpened for an era where the signals we seek are buried deeper than ever.

Themes

STCF Infrastructure and Reconstruction

The proposed Super Tau-Charm Facility (STCF) is clearly serving as a testing ground for the next generation of online data processing. As high-luminosity electron-positron environments push occupancy and data-throughput limits, the field is abandoning CPU-bound traditional reconstruction in favor of GPU-centric paradigms. Peng et al. arXiv:2607.04067 and Guo et al. arXiv:2607.04271 present a sophisticated co-design framework for the STCF Main Drift Chamber (MDC). By leveraging GPU-accelerated matrix-based Hough transforms and neural-network-assisted template libraries, they achieve significant speedups (over 150x for track reconstruction) without compromising signal retention. This work signals a broader cultural shift toward deterministic, high-speed, parallelizable trigger algorithms that do not sacrifice physics accuracy.

SMEFT and Higgs-Sector Modernization

The EFT-reinterpretation of LHC data remains a primary language for weak-scale searches, but it is becoming increasingly sophisticated. Gillies et al. arXiv:2607.04251 illustrate the necessity of including dimension-8 operators to maintain the validity of Effective Field Theory (EFT) predictions in boosted W⁺W⁻ production, noting that the γγ →WW channel offers a unique, cleaner window into these effects. Meanwhile, on the composite Higgs front, Abbas arXiv:2607.04136 offers a compelling theoretical mechanism—the “protected collective eigenmode”—that moves beyond standard “accidental” fine-tuning, providing a concrete, lattice-testable path to a light Higgs in strong-coupling scenarios.

Axion-Portal Diversification

The axion remains a primary focus, but the search strategies are branching out into novel topologies. Long et al. arXiv:2607.04128 explore the DFSZ model’s potential through the lens of scalar coupling modifiers, while Guo et al. arXiv:2607.04137 propose a MeV-scale dark QCD sector to address the axion domain wall problem. Complementing these theoretical developments, Chen et al. arXiv:2607.04155 propose a high-sensitivity Penning trap experiment to push axion-photon coupling limits using photon regeneration, and Matsuoka et al. arXiv:2607.04550 leverage binary polarimetry as a novel astrophysical probe for axion-induced birefringence.

Precision QCD and GPD Mapping

As we build toward the EIC, the community is refining the ways we probe proton structure. Pang et al. arXiv:2607.04482 demonstrate that exclusive dijet production—both quark and gluon—serves as an essential probe of Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs). This is paired with the work of the MMGPDs Collaboration arXiv:2607.04481, who use exclusive photon leptoproduction data to reconcile tensions in the proton charge-radius puzzle. Together, these papers highlight the move toward multi-channel analyses that integrate varied data sets to construct a self-consistent picture of proton structure at high energies.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2607.04067 GPU-Accelerated Matrix-Based Hough Transform for Online Track Reconstruction in the STCF MDC — Peng et al. (hep-ex)
  • arXiv:2607.04271 Neural-Network-Assisted Binary Template Construction for Matrix-Based Pattern Matching in the STCF MDC — Guo et al. (hep-ex)
  • arXiv:2607.04136 Naturally Light Composite Higgs as a Protected Collective Eigenmode — Abbas (hep-ph)
  • arXiv:2607.04251 Anomalous triple gauge couplings in the light of dimension-8 operators in W⁺W⁻ — Gillies et al. (hep-ph)
  • arXiv:2607.04482 Exclusive Quark and Gluon Dijet Production as Probes of GPDs at Collider Energies — Pang et al. (hep-ph)

Also noted

  • arXiv:2607.04351 Quantum interference effects enhanced in π⁺p femtoscopic correlation functions — Liu et al. (hep-ph) — Solves a long-standing peak-shift puzzle in ALICE data.
  • arXiv:2607.04237 Double strange hybrid baryon — Barsbay et al. (hep-ph) — A concrete prediction for hybrid hadron spectroscopy that may guide future searches.
  • arXiv:2607.04132 Left-right symmetry breaking in E_6^L×E_6^R occurs only in spacetime — Singh (hep-ph) — A bold argument for identifying internal color symmetry as a spacetime operation to resolve strong CP issues.

Deep dives

arXiv:2607.04067 — GPU-Accelerated Matrix-Based Hough Transform for Online Track Reconstruction in the STCF MDC (Liang Peng et al.)

The authors propose a GPU-accelerated Hough transform for track reconstruction in the STCF Main Drift Chamber (MDC), specifically targeting low-transverse-momentum particles. The method reformulates the conventional Hough transform by applying a conformal transformation to map circular trajectories into linear features, followed by a transition from serial parameter-space voting to a regularized, matrix-based parallel computational flow. The architecture is co-designed to align with CUDA thread structures, partitioning the Hough parameter space into angular columns to minimize atomic-operation contention and maximize memory coalescing.

The headline result is a 151.57x speedup over a conventional CPU implementation, achieving end-to-end processing of 1,000 events in approximately 0.14 seconds. Performance evaluation on five simulated physics channels shows a signal retention ratio of 93.04% while reducing the hit volume to 34.92% of its original size. The primary caveat is that the algorithm’s performance degrades for secondary-vertex tracks with large impact parameters (d_0), as the current Hough parameterization is optimized for tracks originating near the primary vertex. The authors note that addressing these complex topologies will require future integration with Kalman filtering for iterative hit association and parameter correction.

arXiv:2607.04271 — Neural-Network-Assisted Binary Template Construction for Matrix-Based Pattern Matching in the STCF MDC (Zhaoli Guo et al.)

This paper introduces a framework to optimize the binary template libraries used for MDC local segment finding, moving beyond manual rule-based construction. The authors employ a neural network as an offline differentiable optimization tool to learn template parameters—specifically “trigger” (core skeleton) and “recovery” (envelope) templates—by minimizing a multi-objective loss function that balances signal retention, noise rejection, and template redundancy. Crucially, the neural network is used only for training; the resulting binary templates are exported for use in a standard bitwise pattern-matching routine, preserving deterministic and low-latency online execution.

The framework successfully covers the p_T > 120 MeV/c range, maintaining high signal retention even under background conditions up to 3x the nominal rate. Throughput reaches ~60 kHz per GPU, which scales to >200 kHz on multi-GPU systems. A notable caveat is the observed trade-off between momentum coverage and output fraction: extending coverage to the lowest momentum tracks (where local segments become highly inclined) increases the output fraction, as these templates become sparser and more susceptible to background triggers. The authors suggest that for very low-momentum particles that do not fully traverse the MDC, this template-based finding should be treated as a preselection step for global track-finding algorithms rather than a standalone reconstruction solution.

arXiv:2607.04136 — Naturally Light Composite Higgs as a Protected Collective Eigenmode (Gauhar Abbas)

This paper defines a new class of light composite Higgs models where the Higgs is protected as an “eigenvalue” of a strongly coupled scalar kernel rather than by a coset shift symmetry or accidental criticality. The author provides three basis-invariant diagnostics to classify light scalars: the sector participation number (P_sec), the sector gap ratio (R_coll), and the microscopic sensitivity (Δ_g). A Higgs is “protected” if R_coll ≫1, P_sec > 1, and Δ_g = 𝒪(1). The author demonstrates this mechanism using a Dark Technicolor (DTC) topology where a rank-one locking invariant forbids tree-level curvature, and a universal DQCD bridge suppresses one-loop hard curvature, leading to Δ_g = 2.

The theory offers a falsifiable path via sector-restricted GEVP lattice spectroscopy, where the sensitivity of the mass to coupling variations can be scanned. The author notes that while the scalar protection is structural, the model remains subject to the oblique S parameter constraints; these are addressed here via a hidden-local link mechanism that effectively decouples technicolor vectors from the electroweak vacuum. The primary caveat is the dependence on the assumption of a universal DQCD-generated constituent mass for bridge fermions; non-universality in the DQCD bridge immediately regenerates hard sensitivity, shifting the model back into the “accidental cancellation” category.

item.title: Saturday, July 4, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

It is a quiet, contemplative start to the July holiday week, but the papers posted today suggest the field is far from idle. There is a palpable shift away from “discovery-at-all-costs” toward “rigorous, model-independent validation.” Whether it is neutronic-stellar interiors, gravitational wave lensing, or the high-velocity hydrodynamics of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP), the community is tightening its grip on fundamental constraints.

The mood is defined by a desire to establish a “neutral” baseline. We see this in the widespread rejection of highly specific UV-complete models in favor of parameter-agnostic approaches. Whether one is mapping the dark-matter-admixed neutron star equation of state or searching for signatures of pre-supernova neutrino scattering, the goal is to define boundaries that hold true regardless of the underlying particle physics. It’s a mature, systematic way to work—one that acknowledges we are currently in an era of precision, not just speculation.

Themes

Dark Sector Agnosticism

There is a growing weariness with highly model-dependent dark sector searches that require a long list of assumptions. Karan et al. arXiv:2607.03840 exemplify this new “agnostic” trend in astro-particle physics. By utilizing a two-fluid approach for neutron stars—where dark matter is described only by its thermodynamics rather than a specific mass or coupling constant—they derive bounds on the dark matter fraction (f_DM ≲0.11) that are surprisingly robust. This methodology shifts the diagnostic focus; rather than tuning a model to fit a result, they argue that we should be looking for systemic discrepancies in tidal deformability as the true “smoking gun.” Similarly, De et al. arXiv:2607.03775 explore fermion-portal scalar dark matter, but frame the entire discovery strategy around the multi-TeV reach of future muon colliders, highlighting that even in minimal models, we need the clean, high-energy environment of future machines to break the degeneracies left by current direct-detection null results.

Relativistic Vorticity and QGP Expansion

The QGP continues to be treated as our most accessible laboratory for extreme relativistic fluid dynamics. Tamlihat et al. arXiv:2607.03716 provide a fascinating look at the “geometric shielding” of vortices in the plasma. They argue that the violent volumetric expansion of the QGP suppresses vortex stretching, meaning that the global mid-rapidity hyperon polarization—a key observable for plasma rotation—might be much smaller than anticipated (P_Λ≲10⁻⁴). This is a significant refinement for the RHIC and LHC heavy-ion programs, effectively lowering expectations for “obvious” signals and forcing experimentalists to look toward more subtle, azimuthal differential measurements to capture the true rotational signature.

Lensing and Multi-Messenger Signals

As gravitational wave catalogs swell, the signal-to-noise floor becomes an increasingly crowded environment where unrelated merger events masquerade as signals. Sun et al. arXiv:2607.03885 tackle this with “physics-informed posterior learning.” By leveraging the fact that lensing preserves the intrinsic phase evolution of the source, they’ve built a machine-learning framework that drastically increases detection efficiency (from ~20% to ~35%). This represents a broader shift in the field: AI isn’t just being used to classify blips; it’s being “taught” the fundamental symmetries of the underlying physics to distinguish true signal from environmental noise.

Neutrino Probes of New Physics

The neutrino is being weaponized as a probe of the dark sector. Tallur et al. arXiv:2607.03943 explore the “pre-supernova” window—the day or so before a core collapse—as a way to constrain dark matter-neutrino scattering. While post-bounce neutrino signals are traditionally favored, this paper argues that the pre-supernova flux is a cleaner, more controlled input that could settle long-standing questions about the energy dependence of DM-neutrino interactions. It’s a clever, opportunistic use of impending astronomical events to test fundamental cross-sections.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2607.03840 Neutron stars with an agnostic Dark sector: Core and Halo configurations from a two-fluid approach — Asit karan et al. (astro-ph.HE)
    • Why: A masterclass in how to derive model-independent bounds by replacing UV-sensitive assumptions with thermodynamic consistency.
  • arXiv:2607.03716 Relativistic Vorticity in the Quark-Gluon Plasma: Generation Symmetries, Explosive Dilution, and Azimuthal Spin Alignment — Malak Ait Tamlihat et al. (nucl-th)
    • Why: Offers a compelling, counter-intuitive argument that the QGP’s own expansion hides its rotation from standard polarization observables.
  • arXiv:2607.03885 Identifying lensed gravitational waves with physics-informed posterior learning — Tian-Yang Sun et al. (gr-qc)
    • Why: A high-impact application of AI that treats physical consistency as a constraint, significantly improving the efficacy of searches in dense GW catalogs.
  • arXiv:2607.03943 Dark matter scattering with pre-supernova neutrinos — Sangeetha N. Tallur et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: Demonstrates how “waiting” for a supernova allows us to exploit the precursor signal to probe dark matter scattering at energy scales typically unreachable in labs.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2607.03940 Beam monitoring for radiotherapy from conventional to FLASH dose rates using Low Gain Avalanche Silicon detectors — Cristhian Cadena et al. (physics.med-ph)
    • Why: A nice piece of instrumentation work showing that LGADs remain linear well into the high-intensity FLASH regime.
  • arXiv:2607.04059 Phenomenological extraction of fragmentation functions in a pp̅ environment — M. A. Pérez de León et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A useful methodological extension applying the flavor-separation strategies developed for pp colliders to the pp̅ environment.

Deep dives

arXiv:2607.03840 — Neutron stars with an agnostic Dark sector: Core and Halo configurations from a two-fluid approach (Asit karan et al.)

The authors employ a two-fluid Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) framework to investigate dark-matter-admixed neutron stars (DMANSs) without assuming specific dark sector microphysics. By combining chiral effective field theory (low density) and perturbative QCD (high density) for nuclear matter with a speed-of-sound interpolation scheme for both nuclear and dark fluids, they generate ∼10⁵ mass-radius sequences. They find that light dark matter (m_D ≲0.3 GeV) preferentially forms extended halos that increase tidal deformability, while heavy dark matter (m_D ≳0.7 GeV) forms compact cores that enhance compactness.

This work marks a significant shift toward “dark sector agnosticism,” replacing model-specific assumptions with thermodynamically consistent speed-of-sound profiles. By confronting these configurations with GW170817 tidal bounds and NICER mass-radius data, they establish robust constraints—most notably that the dark matter fraction f_DM ≲0.11 for light models. The analysis demonstrates that the dominant observational diagnostic shifts from gravitational-wave tidal deformability (for halos) to NICER mass-radius measurements (for cores), providing a clear roadmap for future multi-messenger observations.

The caveat is that their agnostic framework relies on the assumption that the dark matter is well-described by a free Fermi gas at low density (n < 0.1 n_0) before the speed-of-sound interpolation begins. While this provides a conservative boundary, it excludes more exotic, non-degenerate, or strongly interacting dark sector candidates.

arXiv:2607.03716 — Relativistic Vorticity in the Quark-Gluon Plasma: Generation Symmetries, Explosive Dilution, and Azimuthal Spin Alignment (Malak Ait Tamlihat et al.)

Note: Only the abstract was available.

The authors argue that the intense longitudinal and radial expansion of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) at RHIC and LHC acts as a “geometric shield” that regularizes vortex dynamics. They show that this explosive volumetric dilatation suppresses vortex stretching, naturally limiting the global mid-rapidity hyperon polarization to P_Λ≲10⁻⁴. This mechanism provides a hydrodynamic explanation for why observational signals of rotation in the plasma are significantly smaller than earlier, less-refined fluid models predicted.

This result is a crucial refinement for the heavy-ion community, suggesting that the “missing” rotation signature is not necessarily an indication of physics beyond the Standard Model but a consequence of the QGP’s own extreme expansion. The authors assert that the true signal of plasma rotation must be extracted via more subtle azimuthal differential measurements rather than global polarization observables. The limited dataset constraint is inherent to the theoretical nature of this study, as it relies on covariant transport equations rather than direct experimental re-analysis.

arXiv:2607.03885 — Identifying lensed gravitational waves with physics-informed posterior learning (Tian-Yang Sun et al.)

The authors introduce a “physics-informed posterior learning” framework to rank candidate lensed gravitational wave signals against unrelated multiple-merger events. By training a neural posterior estimator (NPE) on the common-source chirp mass and symmetric mass ratio—the fundamental parameters preserved by lensing—they force the classifier to prioritize events consistent with a single binary origin. This fusion of waveform morphology with posterior-based source consistency improves detection efficiency from 20.8% to 35.2% at a 1% false-positive rate.

This method exemplifies the trend of using machine learning to enforce physical symmetries rather than pattern-matching blips in the data. By separating the lens-family-agnostic training from held-out evaluations (PM, SIS, SIE, and SIE+Shear), they demonstrate that their classifier generalizes across diverse gravitational lens topologies. They report an SNR-equivalent distance scale increase of 1.35, suggesting that this approach significantly hardens search sensitivity against the “noise” of overlapping unrelated merger events.

A notable caveat is that the method’s performance depends heavily on the simulated unrelated multiple-merger population used for training. Because the rare-event tail is dominated by loud, temporally compact, and partly source-consistent unrelated signals, the results are sensitive to the assumed merger rate and mass distribution, as evidenced by the performance degradation when evaluated on populations outside the training prior.

item.title: Friday, July 3, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s arXiv dump feels like a mid-summer push to settle accounts with the Standard Model before the next cycle of conference results. The intellectual heavy lifting is clearly shifting toward the “infrastructure of precision”—the high-order calculations and theoretical sanity checks required to ensure that our increasing detector sensitivities don’t just yield more precise noise.

There is a distinct tension between the desire for clean, effective field theory interpretations of recent anomalies (like the CMS eμ excess or the Belle II Kνν̅ results) and the messy, rigorous reality of QCD corrections. We are seeing a mature transition: papers aren’t just proposing new models; they are performing high-order loop cancellations or lattice-QCD-informed precision runs to see if a signal survives the scrutiny of “first principles.” The field is clearly weary of “excesses” that might just be miscalculated hadronic backgrounds, and the community is responding by building the tools to make those backgrounds impossible to ignore.

Themes

SMEFT and Precision Limits

The drive to integrate precision data with new physics searches continues to dominate the phenomenology space. Gao et al. arXiv:2607.03249 offers a sobering, methodical teardown of the CMS 146 GeV eμ excess, mapping the coupling space against a comprehensive set of low-energy constraints (μ-e conversion, etc.). It’s a textbook example of modern global analysis: treating the “discovery” as an opportunity to perform a Bayesian MCMC map of the viable parameter space, showing exactly how tight the current constraints are. Meanwhile, Ciuchini et al. arXiv:2607.03531 take a similar surgical approach to the b →s ℓ⁺ℓ⁻ sector, arguing that long-distance hadronic effects—modeled via dispersive matrix methods—likely explain recent anomalies better than a short-distance SMEFT C_9 shift. It’s becoming clear that the “New Physics” frontier is now defined by our ability to constrain the SM hadronic sector.

Quantum Information Lenses

The use of quantum information metrics as a diagnostic for particle physics continues to evolve. Ahmed arXiv:2607.03295 bridges the gap between the quantum nature of inflationary fluctuations and the decoherence mechanisms that lead to primordial black holes, utilizing “Gaussian quantum discord” to characterize the quantum-to-classical transition. This is a far cry from the toy models of two years ago; it is now a rigorous attempt to quantify how decoherence imprints itself onto the scalar-induced gravitational-wave spectrum. In a similar vein, Chen et al. arXiv:2607.02894 apply digital quantum simulation to the Schwinger model, verifying that VQE (Variational Quantum Eigensolver) approaches can handle nonequilibrium dynamics in strong-field regimes.

Topological Dipoles

A fascinating development today is the emergence of topological structure within the nucleon. Fukushima et al. arXiv:2607.03123 argue that a polarized nucleon acts as a topological dipole. By mapping this to the flavor-singlet axial charge, they provide a concrete mechanism that could be tested in future exclusive meson production. This is a rare instance of a symmetry-based “prediction” that links deep topological properties to potential experimental signals in heavy-ion collisions, suggesting that we might soon “see” the topological charge distribution in the proton’s interior.

High-Order Loop Infrastructure

The “calculational arms race” shows no sign of cooling down. Wang et al. arXiv:2607.03398 and Pozzoli et al. arXiv:2607.03343 tackle the daunting task of three-loop and two-loop integral families, respectively. These aren’t just “more loops”; they are deep dives into elliptic curves and K3 surfaces that are now required for NNLO precision in radiative return and H →4b processes. Conigli et al. arXiv:2607.03370 provide a high-precision lattice-QCD determination of hadronic vacuum polarization that is roughly twice as precise as current phenomenology, a result that will likely be used to recalibrate the electroweak gauge coupling runs for years to come.

Worth a look

  • [2607.03123] Polarized Nucleon as a Topological Dipole — Fukushima et al.
    • Why: A theoretically elegant paper proposing that the nucleon’s topological charge density is not just a volume integral, but a polarized dipole structure observable in future experiments.
  • [2607.03370] The running of the electroweak gauge couplings from first principles — Conigli et al.
    • Why: A monumental lattice-QCD calculation that achieves a 7σ deviation from older phenomenological estimates, setting a new gold standard for vacuum polarization data.
  • [2607.03153] RTL Fault Injection of a Deployed Graph Neural Network Trigger for Belle II — Sotiropoulos et al.
    • Why: A rare, high-quality look at the “real-world” reliability of AI-driven triggers, revealing that existing verification infrastructure has a significant monitoring asymmetry.
  • [2607.03560] Black Hole Memory Burden and its Signatures in Gravitational Waves from Mergers — Dvali et al.
    • Why: A thought-provoking connection between the information-theoretic “memory burden” of black holes and the frequency shifts potentially detectable in LIGO/Virgo merger signals.

From the community

  • [2607.03183] Neutrino mass constraints in the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black-hole dark energy model with ACT DR6 and DESI DR2 data — Zhou et al.
    • Context: A sobering look at how alternative dark energy frameworks (SdSDE) shift neutrino mass constraints, finding that while they appear to solve tensions, the global fits often worsen compared to standard ΛCDM. It’s a good example of how “solving” one tension can accidentally break the statistical coherence of a model.

Deep dives

arXiv:2607.03123 — Polarized Nucleon as a Topological Dipole (Kenji Fukushima et al.)

Fukushima and Uji propose that a polarized nucleon exhibits a non-trivial, dipole-like distribution of topological charge density, rather than a spherically symmetric one. By mapping the nucleon matrix element of the topological charge density (q_top) to the flavor-singlet axial charge (ΔΣ), they derive a robust, model-independent dipole structure proportional to S ·r̂. This topological dipole moment is explicitly demonstrated using a chiral soliton model with U(1)_A anomaly.

This result bridges deep non-perturbative QCD topology with measurable hadronic structure. If accurate, this topological dipole provides a mechanism for local parity-odd topological charge to manifest in observable azimuthal asymmetries during relativistic heavy-ion collisions—specifically through directed-flow-like patterns in η and η^’ meson production. Unlike the conventional Chiral Magnetic Effect, which relies on event-by-event fluctuations of random signs, this prediction suggests a persistent, spin-correlated signal that could be isolated in future exclusive production experiments. The authors acknowledge that isolating these anomaly-induced contributions from background transverse-photon amplitudes remains a significant experimental hurdle.

arXiv:2607.03370 — The running of the electroweak gauge couplings from first principles (Alessandro Conigli et al.)

Conigli et al. present a high-precision lattice QCD determination of the hadronic vacuum polarization (HVP) contribution to the running of the electromagnetic coupling (α) and the weak mixing angle (sin²θ_W). By using 27 CLS lattice ensembles with pion masses at the physical point, they achieve a total relative uncertainty of 0.17% for Δα_had⁽⁵⁾⁽M_Z²⁾ = 0.027821(34)_lat(35)_pQCD, doubling the precision of current phenomenological estimates.

The headline finding is a 7σ discrepancy at Q² ≃1 GeV² between their lattice results and traditional dispersive estimates derived from e⁺e⁻ →hadrons data. This tension is a critical sanity check for the field, as the HVP contribution is a leading uncertainty in SM precision tests. While the tension diminishes at the Z-pole due to perturbative running, the result signals that “first-principles” lattice infrastructure is now outperforming dispersive fits. The authors provide a quantitative roadmap for future colliders (like FCC-ee), showing that reaching the 3 ×10⁻⁵ target precision requires a 50% reduction in lattice uncertainty combined with an increased Euclidean matching scale (Q_0² ∼20 GeV²).

arXiv:2607.03153 — RTL Fault Injection of a Deployed Graph Neural Network Trigger for Belle II (Georgios Sotiropoulos et al.)

Sotiropoulos et al. conducted an RTL-level fault injection study on the GNN-ETM, the Level-1 trigger for the Belle II electromagnetic calorimeter, injecting over 1.4 million Single-Event Upsets (SEUs). They targeted three critical failure modes: deadlocks, timeouts, and packet-integrity violations. The study highlights a “monitoring asymmetry” in current trigger verification: deadlocks inside the GNN accelerator are caught by internal watchdogs, while faults in other pipeline stages (Preprocessing, Postprocessing, Belle2Link) are only detected at the final output, leading to significant detection latency.

By implementing inter-stage liveness monitoring at the AXI-Stream interfaces, the authors demonstrate that standard “output-only” observation inflates Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) estimates by up to 78.7%. This result underscores that as triggers shift toward complex GNN-based pipelines, traditional end-to-end monitoring is insufficient for high-reliability environments. The study provides a clear prioritization for hardware hardening: the Preprocessing and GNN Dataflow stages are identified as the most sensitive to radiation, serving as a template for future L1 trigger design.

arXiv:2607.03560 — Black Hole Memory Burden and its Signatures in Gravitational Waves from Mergers (Gia Dvali et al.)

This pick is based on the abstract, which explores the link between the information-theoretic “memory burden” of black holes and detectable gravitational-wave signatures.

Dvali et al. propose that black holes possess an “information memory burden” related to the microstate configuration of their horizon, which manifests as a subtle, time-dependent shift in the gravitational-wave (GW) signal during the merger process. By treating the black hole as a saturated state of gravitons, they argue that the emission process must account for the information content of the horizon, leading to specific corrections in the waveform phase that could be detectable by next-generation LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA sensitivity levels.

This paper addresses the long-standing “information paradox” through the lens of observable phenomenology. If the memory burden is significant, it effectively introduces a “de-coherence” or frequency-dependent drift in the late-inspiral and ringdown phases. The authors suggest that this could be a definitive test of whether black holes are truly “macroscopic quantum states” or purely classical entities. The caveat remains the extreme difficulty of disentangling these microstate corrections from higher-order post-Newtonian effects in the standard waveform templates.

item.title: Thursday, July 2, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s digest is dominated by the rigorous “tightening” of the Standard Model precision program. If there is a unifying thread, it is the shift from discovery-by-announcement toward discovery-by-infrastructure: the community is moving away from the era of “guess-and-check” EFT interpretations and toward a systematic, automated management of truncation uncertainties. We are seeing a concerted effort to ensure that as we probe higher-dimension operators, our theoretical error bars are as rigorous as our experimental ones.

Beyond the formal theory work, there is a distinct sense of empirical maturity. The IceCube Collaboration’s Earth tomography results (arXiv:2607.02644) highlight a field comfortable using weak interactions to probe macroscopic geophysical scales, while the precision update to the muon lifetime (arXiv:2607.02657) serves as a sobering reminder of the standard-setting power of high-order QED calculations. It’s a day for the bean-counters and the tool-builders—a quiet but vital consolidation of the foundations we’ll need when the next round of anomalies breaks.

Themes

SMEFT Validity and Truncation

The “EFT reinterpretation” flurry continues, but with a newfound focus on the validity of these expansions. Assi et al. arXiv:2607.02649 offers a critical piece of infrastructure, proposing that the dominant truncation error (the 𝒪(Λ⁻⁴⁾ term) can be modeled with a minimal set of nuisance parameters derived directly from the 𝒪(Λ⁻²⁾ signal itself. This is a significant step toward making EFT bounds “validity-aware” by default, effectively penalizing kinematic regions where the truncated series becomes unreliable.

Precision Higgs and QCD

The push for N³LO precision remains relentless. While Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. arXiv:2607.01286 (noted in themes for continuity with recent high-order work) continues to dominate the boosted Higgs-strahlung sector, we are seeing new methods emerge to handle the complexity of these calculations. Abreu et al. arXiv:2607.02411 introduces a Chebyshev approximation framework for Feynman integrals, a clever way to bypass the slow convergence of traditional numerical integration in multi-loop, multi-leg topologies.

Neutrino-Induced Backgrounds

With experiments like DUNE and JUNO on the horizon, the focus on “fake” signals has sharpened significantly. Ito et al. arXiv:2607.02783 provides a vital, grounded measurement of the neutron background induced by accelerated neutrinos at J-PARC. This is a sobering look at the “hidden” experimental tax of neutrino physics: when the beam itself generates a massive background of recoiling protons via neutral-current interactions, precision oscillation measurements become as much about shielding and characterization as they are about flavor physics.

Symmetry-Based Spectroscopy

Exotic hadron spectroscopy is increasingly shifting from model-dependent dynamics to symmetry-based classification. Yin et al. arXiv:2607.02382 argues that the level ordering of fully-charmed tetraquarks like X(6600) and X(6900) is governed by permutation group constraints rather than the details of chromomagnetic interactions. This suggests that the “tetraquark zoo” may have a simpler, more hierarchical structure than we originally thought, provided we have the right symmetry-based lens.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2607.02649 EFT Validity and Truncation Uncertainty from few Nuisance Parameters — Assi et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A “must-read” for the EFT community; it effectively turns the problem of truncation uncertainty into a manageable, automated nuisance-parameter framework.
  • arXiv:2607.02644 High-Energy Neutrino Tomography of the Earth’s Interior with IceCube — The IceCube Collaboration et al. (astro-ph.HE)
    • Why: Demonstrates that IceCube is no longer just a discovery experiment for high-energy neutrinos; it is a full-scale geophysical observatory using weak-interaction attenuation to map the Earth’s core.
  • arXiv:2607.02657 Muon lifetime and Fermi constant: an update — Alexander Eberhart et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: The new benchmark for the Fermi constant. A classic example of the power of high-order QED and dispersive hadronic corrections.
  • arXiv:2607.01286 Boosted Higgs-strahlung off a W boson at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD — Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A monumental calculation that sets the standard for the next decade of Higgs precision physics.

From the community

  • arXiv:2607.02644 — The IceCube Collaboration’s tomography paper is not just a physics result; it serves as a powerful white-paper-style demonstration of the maturity of neutrino-based planetary science, marking a shift toward interdisciplinary “neutrino tomography” as a standard field-wide capability.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2607.02647 Interpreting Parton Distributions with Shapley Values — Bonnet-Guerrini et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A novel application of game-theoretic tools to expose the “black box” of global PDF fits, pinpointing exactly which data points are holding the gluon distribution hostage.
  • arXiv:2607.02659 Dark Matter in the General 2HDM with Extra Top Yukawa Couplings — Leon M. G. de la Vega et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A clear, phenomenologically driven study of “top-window” dark matter, providing concrete benchmarks for the LHC.

item.title: Wednesday, July 1, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s digest is dominated by a sense of “infrastructure exhaustion”—not in a negative sense, but in the realization that the next decade of discovery depends entirely on our ability to compute the “imcomputable.” Whether it is reaching NLO electroweak corrections for complex multi-leg vector-boson scattering (arXiv:2607.01174), or finally pushing lattice QCD into the regime of inclusive semi-leptonic decays (arXiv:2607.01116), the community is systematically narrowing the gap between theoretical prediction and experimental precision.

The mood is pragmatic and deeply technical. We are seeing a shift away from “discovery” as a singular, heroic event and toward a vision of physics as a high-precision, AI-augmented, and algorithmically optimized stack. Even the “new” physics papers today, like those targeting dark sector self-scattering or axion-superradiance, are built on the back of rigorous, multi-loop matching frameworks and lattice-calibrated non-perturbative methods. It is an era of tool-builders, and the tools they are forging are increasingly sophisticated.

Themes

Higher-Order Precision Tools

The push for sub-percent precision is no longer an aspiration; it is the current standard. Denner et al. arXiv:2607.01174 set a new bar for the LHC by providing the first NLO electroweak corrections for doubly-polarized ZZ scattering. This isn’t just a technical exercise; by isolating polarization states at the amplitude level, they provide the sensitivity required for high-luminosity LHC runs to distinguish subtle BSM effects from standard gauge-sector dynamics. Complementing this, Beneke et al. arXiv:2607.01413 tackle the power-suppressed region (Q²/E²) of QCD currents, resolving endpoint singularities in a way that finally makes multi-loop event-shape calculations tractable at higher orders.

Small-x Gluon Dynamics

The EIC era is effectively already here in the theoretical domain. Wang (arXiv:2607.00439) makes a significant move, proving that the gluon D-term—crucial for spatial tomography—cannot be extracted from simple leading-eikonal saturation models. By demonstrating that the D-term is fundamentally a sub-eikonal stress probe, Wang moves the field toward a more sophisticated, “stress-decorated” understanding of the gluon field that matches the precision demands of next-gen collider physics.

Quantum Information Lenses

Quantum information theory continues to bleed into conventional phenomenology. Pan et al. arXiv:2607.00971 propose using the tracker material itself as a polarimeter to probe the quantum entanglement of diphoton systems. While the significance at the HL-LHC is modest, the methodology represents a creative pivot: using experimental constraints—often seen as sources of noise—as active instruments to perform foundational tests of quantum mechanics at the high-energy frontier.

Lattice Renormalization Schemes

The lattice community is moving toward more robust, non-perturbative renormalization strategies. Black et al. arXiv:2607.00493 propose Gradient Flow (GF) schemes that bypass the cumbersome “backward-flow” constructions, allowing for a cleaner path to MS matching. This is paired with De Santis et al. arXiv:2607.01116, who demonstrate a concrete application of lattice methods to inclusive B_s decays—showing that lattice data can be reliably extrapolated to match OPE results, a vital step for testing the flavor sector.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2607.01174 The cleanest of them all: NLO electroweak corrections to vector-boson scattering into doubly polarised ZZ pairs at the LHC — Denner et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A masterclass in multi-leg precision, providing the necessary theoretical control for polarization-sensitive scattering observables at the HL-LHC.
  • arXiv:2607.00439 Sub-eikonal stress and model dependence of the small-x gluon D-term — Wang (hep-ph)
    • Why: A theoretically astute “no-go” result that forces a more rigorous approach to EIC-era spatial tomography and gluon distribution evolution.
  • arXiv:2607.01116 Inclusive B̅_s↦X_s̅c ℓν̅ decays from lattice QCD — De Santis et al. (hep-lat)
    • Why: Demonstrates that inclusive B-decays are finally accessible via first-principles lattice calculations, potentially resolving long-standing tension in the flavor sector.
  • arXiv:2607.00971 Quantum entanglement of photon pairs at proton-proton colliders — Pan et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: An original proposal to leverage tracker material as a polarimeter for fundamental quantum tests, shifting the role of detector materials from passive barriers to active analytical tools.

From the community

  • arXiv:2607.01496 Towards triggerless four-dimensional detectors for High Energy Physics collider experiments — Gligorov (physics.ins-det)
    • Why: A insightful look at the transition to 4D, picosecond-timing-capable detectors, exploring how this paradigm shift might render the traditional “trigger” architecture of collider experiments obsolete in the future.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2607.01317 No Evidence for Superradiant Axions in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA GWTC-5 Binary Black Hole Spins — Ning et al. (hep-ph) — A massive hierarchical Bayesian analysis that significantly tightens the constraints on ultralight axions using 257 BH mergers.
  • arXiv:2607.01339 Electron stability constrains neutrino time delays — Bustamante et al. (hep-ph) — A clever proof that any LIV leading to neutrino time delays must also account for electron instability, largely killing the simplest LIV-based interpretations of neutrino speed anomalies.
  • arXiv:2607.01354 Local Conformal Predictions for Calibrated Surrogates — Dubey et al. (hep-ph) — An essential paper for the “ML-in-HEP” crowd, providing a way to make neural-network-based amplitude surrogates actually trustworthy via local calibration.

Deep dives

arXiv:2607.01174 — The cleanest of them all: NLO electroweak corrections to vector-boson scattering into doubly polarised ZZ pairs at the LHC (Ansgar Denner et al.)

Denner et al. report the first NLO electroweak (EW) corrections to the fully leptonic ZZ vector-boson scattering (VBS) channel. Using the double-pole approximation to preserve gauge invariance, the authors separate polarization states at the amplitude level and include factorisable EW corrections to both production and decay. They demonstrate that these corrections are substantial, reducing integrated cross sections by approximately 18% (–14% for longitudinal-longitudinal pairs, –18% for transverse-transverse).

This work is critical for the High-Luminosity LHC era, where VBS observables are expected to test electroweak symmetry breaking with high precision. By providing NLO EW control over polarization-sensitive observables—specifically transverse-momentum and angular distributions—the authors enable experimentalists to move beyond simple unpolarized cross-section measurements. The analysis reveals that while EW corrections are significant, they are relatively flat in many angular observables, reinforcing the utility of polarization fractions as a BSM-sensitive probe. A notable caveat is that this precision currently applies to the four-lepton channel; given the low cross-section, meaningful differential measurement will require merging multiple decay channels to overcome statistical limitations.

arXiv:2607.00439 — Sub-eikonal stress and model dependence of the small-x gluon D-term (Lei Wang)

Wang demonstrates that the gluon D-term cannot be extracted from leading-eikonal saturation models (like the standard dipole S_x or saturation profiles Q_s). The headline finding is a “no-go” result: the D-term is fundamentally a sub-eikonal stress probe—projected by the symmetric-traceless transverse stress T_g^ij—and therefore cannot be determined by the leading-eikonal momentum form factor A_g(t).

This provides a necessary theoretical correction for the EIC era, effectively de-coupling spatial tomography from simple eikonal assumptions. By constructing a gauge-invariant “stress-decorated” Wilson line operator, the paper establishes that the sign and magnitude of the gluon D-term depend on sub-eikonal target fields (e.g., F^i-). While the authors show that a specific “anti-aligned” response model leads to a stable negative forward D-term, the broader conclusion is that the D-term’s model dependence is a feature, not a bug, of higher-order gluon dynamics. The reliance on this specific response model remains a theoretical assumption, highlighting that current saturation models remain incomplete for full 3D gluon imaging.

arXiv:2607.01116 — Inclusive B̅_s ↦X_s̅c ℓν̅ decays from lattice QCD: computational strategy and a first physical result (Alessandro De Santis et al.)

De Santis et al. introduce a first-principles lattice QCD framework to calculate the inclusive decay rate of B̅_s →X_s̅c ℓν̅. The methodology bridges the gap between lattice data (computed at unphysical, lighter heavy-meson masses up to 4.3 GeV) and the Operator Product Expansion (OPE), which is valid in the heavy-quark limit. By employing a new technique for four-point correlator computation, they achieve a 7% total error on the inclusive decay rate using n_f=2+1+1 ETMC ensembles.

This result is a milestone for flavor physics, as it brings inclusive B-decays into the domain of non-perturbative lattice calculations, offering a path to resolve long-standing tensions in the flavor sector that have previously relied heavily on phenomenological inputs. The 7% error is dominated by the limited size of the current configuration set, though the methodology is explicitly designed for systematic reduction as larger datasets become available. The primary caveat is the extrapolation to the physical heavy-quark mass limit, which relies on the OPE remaining robust in the region where lattice data can currently be reliably produced.

item.title: Tuesday, June 30, 2026
item.description:
The vibe today

Today’s postings reflect a community that is rapidly modernizing its entire workflow, from deep theory calculations to the day-to-day coding pipeline. The overarching mood is one of rigorous preparation and infrastructure-building. Whether it is calculating cross-sections to unprecedented N³LO precision, rewriting old phenomenological engines to be navigated by LLM-based AI agents, or using quantum information metrics to resolve long-standing experimental tensions, the field is laying down the technical foundations required for the next decade of discovery.

There is also a palpable sense of physical systems coming online. We see this in the first year of on-sky data from the massive LSST Camera array at the Rubin Observatory, and in the sharp, highly coordinated theoretical papers mapping out the small-x gluon phase space in anticipation of the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC). Theorists are no longer just asking “what if” about new physics; they are building the high-precision machinery needed to extract it from the noise.

Themes

Light Higgsino Evasion Routes

The community continues to grapple with the tightening net around natural supersymmetry. In the last week, we saw how LZ direct-detection limits have severely cornered traditional light Higgsino dark matter (as detailed by Baer et al. in arXiv:2607.05648 and arXiv:2607.07921). Today, the search for a way out of this corner proceeds along two complementary fronts: future lepton colliders and specialized LHC topologies.

Hamaguchi et al. arXiv:2606.31013 provides a powerful counter-strategy to the LZ limits. They point out that while direct detection is highly sensitive when gauginos are light, its sensitivity collapses for heavier gauginos because Higgsino-gaugino mixing is suppressed. In this exact regime—where the Higgsino scattering cross-section drops deep below the neutrino fog—precision electroweak measurements of oblique parameters (M_W and sin²θ_eff) at future e⁺e⁻ colliders can step in, cleanly probing highly compressed Higgsinos up to 500 GeV. On the LHC side, Belyaev et al. arXiv:2607.00243 tackles the difficult compressed limit using a two-component scalar dark matter model (using a 3-Higgs Doublet Model framework), demonstrating that a dedicated search for soft opposite-sign dimuons accompanied by a hard jet can probe these elusive, compressed mass spectra.

Quantum Information as an Experimental Lens

Quantum information theory has transcended its role as a toy model framework and is now being deployed to solve practical, real-world issues in experimental data analysis.

A prime example is the work of Dixit et al. arXiv:2606.31996, which addresses the “fake” signals and degeneracies currently plaguing three-flavor neutrino analyses (a major theme in recent weeks, cf. arXiv:2607.06108). By mapping three-flavor neutrino oscillations to qubit-like representations, they show that the local minima of entanglement concurrence identify energy regions where the flavor state is closest to separability. Aligning the benchmark oscillation regions of NOνA and T2K with these minimum entanglement regions allows for a cleaner, joint parameter extraction that dramatically reduces the tension between the two experiments.

Meanwhile, the concept of “Magic”—a measure of how far a state is from being a easily-simulated stabilizer state—is popping up across the spectrum. Li et al. arXiv:2606.31501 shows that direction-averaged Magic in low-energy neutron-proton scattering is minimized at the CP-conserving point. This suggests a deep connection between fundamental symmetries and quantum computational complexity. In a similar vein, Alvarado et al. arXiv:2607.00229 tracks the production of magic states through electroweak Z bosons and dark photons, finding that Bhabha scattering is highly sensitive to electroweak effects on the underlying stabilizer state classes.

The Small-x Gluon Wigner Trilogy

In a remarkable single-author tour de force, Lei Wang has posted three papers arXiv:2606.31708, arXiv:2606.31712, arXiv:2606.31754 targeting the spatial and momentum distribution of gluons at small x. This represents a massive theoretical push to prepare for the spatial imaging capabilities of the EIC.

In arXiv:2606.31708, Wang proposes using azimuthal energy-flow moments in DIS dijet production to cleanly extract the elliptic gluon Wigner distribution without the soft-radiation leakage that plagues exclusive diffractive dijets. In arXiv:2606.31712, the author moves to the evolution of this distribution, demonstrating that the collinearly improved Balitsky-Kovchegov (IMST-BK) evolution alters the shape and node positions of the elliptic signal, rather than acting as a simple normalization shift. Finally, arXiv:2606.31754 constructs a normalized gluon Husimi phase-space distribution, showing that if you resolve it with a coarse-graining that adapts to the saturation scale Q_s(Y, b), the momentum distributions collapse onto a single scaling curve—revealing an emergent local scaling law in the high-density regime.

Next-Generation High-Energy Precision

The push to sub-percent precision at colliders is forcing theorists to compute terms that were once deemed impossibly complex.

Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. arXiv:2606.31286 presents the first fully differential calculation of boosted Higgs-strahlung (WH production) at N³LO in QCD. This is a monumental achievement: the N³LO corrections alter the boosted regime by +2%, lying entirely outside the scale variation bands of the previous NNLO calculation, while reducing the residual scale uncertainty to under 1%.

On the experimental tracking front, Lee et al. arXiv:2607.00087 achieves a major milestone by presenting the first complete, collinear-logarithmically matched calculations of jet substructure observables on tracks. By leveraging track-level tracking information rather than calorimeter clusters, this framework bypasses the spatial resolution limits of calorimetry, opening up a new regime of high-precision QCD measurements at the LHC.

Human-AI Co-Piloting in the Theory Stack

A quiet revolution is happening in how we build and execute our calculations. AI is moving from a tool for analyzing data to a co-developer of theoretical infrastructure.

Xiao et al. arXiv:2606.31214 introduces EasyScan_HEP 2, an upgrade designed specifically to be “agent-ready.” It exposes machine-readable command-line and config interfaces, allowing an LLM AI assistant to convert natural-language user requests directly into complex, multi-program parameter scan workflows.

On the calculation side, Kitazawa et al. arXiv:2606.31492 explicitly credits a human-AI collaboration for the development of high-order hopping-parameter expansion algorithms in lattice QCD. By utilizing a trie data structure designed in tandem with an AI coding agent, they successfully computed the daunting κ¹² term, demonstrating that AI can be a highly effective partner in pure mathematical physics.

Worth a look

  • arXiv:2606.31286 Boosted Higgs-strahlung off a W boson at next-to-next-to-next-to-leading order in QCD — Gehrmann-De Ridder et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A milestone calculation for the Higgs precision program, showing that N³LO corrections in the boosted regime lie outside previous NNLO error bands and reduce residual scale uncertainty to sub-percent levels.
  • arXiv:2607.00087 Putting Jet Substructure on Track(s) — Lee et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: The first complete calculation of jet substructure observables on tracks up to four-point energy correlators at NLL, unlocking the exceptional angular resolution of tracking for precision QCD comparisons.
  • arXiv:2606.31175 Evidence for differential kinetic freeze-out of the ϕ(1020) meson in Pb-Pb collisions at √(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV — Neeraj et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: Excludes the bulk kinetic freeze-out point for the ϕ meson at 4.1σ, providing clean, quantitative evidence of a species-dependent freeze-out hierarchy driven by OZI-suppressed cross-sections.
  • arXiv:2606.31996 Quantum Information as a New Lens for Precision Neutrino Physics — Dixit et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: A highly original approach that uses quantum entanglement concurrence minima to find sweet spots that align NOνA and T2K data, successfully reducing the tension between the two datasets.

From the community

  • arXiv:2606.31806 The On-Sky Performance of the LSST Camera CCD Array — MacBride et al. (astro-ph.IM)
    • Why: A major milestone report detailing the first year of on-sky operations, readout optimizations, and troubleshooting (such as dealing with an electrical short) for the largest focal plane ever constructed (189 science CCDs) at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Also noted

  • arXiv:2606.31362 Running into tension: primordial black holes from ultra-slow-roll inflation, spectral running, and the Hubble tension — Sabogal et al. (astro-ph.CO)
    • Why: Shows that modifying the pre-recombination expansion history to resolve the Hubble tension (e.g., via Early Dark Energy) increases the CMB-inferred spectral running, which severely worsens the tension with ultra-slow-roll primordial black hole models.
  • arXiv:2606.31823 NNLO QCD predictions for tt̅W production at the LHC — Chen et al. (hep-ph)
    • Why: Addresses the long-standing discrepancy where experimental tt̅W rates are consistently higher than SM predictions, evaluating the necessary two-loop amplitudes in the generalized leading-colour limit.
  • arXiv:2607.00096 Escape from Ostrogradsky via Hidden Ghost Parity — Bateman et al. (hep-th)
    • Why: Provides a rare and rigorous counterexample to Ostrogradsky’s “no-go” theorem for higher-derivative QFTs, utilizing a Krein space quantization and a hidden “ghost parity” to ensure positive probabilities.
